edges.effect_quant: The most useful pooled estimate comes from a 2015 meta-analysis of 423 infants, where Lactobacillus reuteri DSM 17938 improved treatment response at 2 weeks (RR 2.84, 95% CI 1.24-6.50) and cut crying time by about 43 to 46 minutes per day over weeks 2 to 3. A newer 2024 review still found a DSM 17938 subgroup crying-time reduction of about 64.66 minutes per day.
edges.population: mostly breastfed infants younger than 3 months with infant colic
edges.mechanism: Lactobacillus reuteri DSM 17938 may reduce infant colic by shifting gut fermentation patterns, lowering ammonia and Escherichia coli burden, and improving gut motility and visceral comfort during early infancy.
edges.summary: The strongest direct evidence still supports Lactobacillus reuteri DSM 17938 as a helpful option for breastfed infants with colic. The signal is not universal across every feeding pattern, but the better trials and pooled data consistently show less crying time and higher responder rates in the subgroup that drives most real-world use.
edges.caveats: Most of the benefit signal comes from breastfed infants, and some later formula-fed or mixed-intervention studies have been less convincing. This edge should be read as strain-specific and subgroup-sensitive rather than a blanket probiotic effect for every colicky infant.
